title: 3.4 Bioenergetic Limiting Factors in Exercise Performance

cards.front: Why is understanding bioenergetic limiting factors necessary when designing athletic training programs?
cards.back: Identifying the specific limiting factors associated with a particular athletic event is required to design targeted training programs that delay fatigue, mitigate substrate depletion, and enhance exercise performance.

cards.front: For which types of exercise is glycogen depletion a major bioenergetic limiting factor?
cards.back:
Glycogen depletion limits performance during both:
  • Long-duration, low-intensity exercise supported primarily by aerobic metabolism.
  • Repeated, high-intensity exercise supported primarily by anaerobic mechanisms.

cards.front: How does metabolic acidosis (H+ accumulation) limit exercise performance in anaerobic activities?
cards.back: Accumulation of hydrogen ions (H+) reduces intracellular pH, directly limiting contractile force during sprinting, resistance training, and other anaerobic activities by inhibiting glycolytic enzymes and disrupting crossbridge recycling.

cards.front: How does increased intracellular inorganic phosphate (Pi) contribute to muscle fatigue?
cards.back: Elevated intracellular inorganic phosphate (Pi) from rapid ATP hydrolysis directly impairs calcium (Ca2+) release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and reduces myofilament force production.

cards.front: What metabolic process causes ammonia accumulation, and how does it affect fatigue?
cards.back: Ammonia accumulates as a result of AMP deamination (via the adenylate kinase reaction) and amino acid degradation during intense exercise. Accumulating ammonia exerts toxic effects that contribute to peripheral and central muscular fatigue.

cards.front: How does creatine phosphate (CP) depletion limit maximal high-intensity exercise?
cards.back: Rapid depletion of intramuscular creatine phosphate (CP) severely restricts the rate of ATP resynthesis, limiting maximal power output during short-duration, high-intensity explosive activities (0 to 30 seconds).

cards.front: How does impaired calcium (Ca2+) release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum cause fatigue?
cards.back: Impaired sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release reduces cytosolic calcium availability, directly dampening troponin binding, crossbridge activation, and muscle contractile force.

cards.front: What effect does increased intracellular ADP concentration have on muscle contraction kinetics?
cards.back: High intracellular ADP concentrations reduce the free energy change available from ATP hydrolysis and slow crossbridge detachment rates, contributing to muscular fatigue.

cards.front: What are the two main categories of bioenergetic factors that limit exercise performance?
cards.back:
• Energy Source Depletion: Depletion of phosphagens (ATP/CP) and muscle/liver glycogen.
  • Metabolic Byproduct Accumulation: Accumulation of hydrogen ions (H+), inorganic phosphate (Pi), ammonia, and ADP.

cards.front: How do bioenergetic limiting factors differ between a maximal sprint and a marathon?
cards.back:
• Maximal Sprint: Limited primarily by phosphagen depletion and metabolic acidosis (H+ accumulation).
  • Marathon: Limited primarily by muscle and liver glycogen depletion and dehydration/thermoregulatory stress.
